title: Four protective meditations
hook: phone, keys, wallet. and four short thoughts for the road.
tomorrow: forty ways to meditate. why so many, and which one is yours?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four elements: hard, fluid, warm, moving, and none of it signed with a name. Today, four of another kind, small enough to fit on one hand.

Phone, keys, wallet: the little pat-down at the front door. Which four thoughts could go out the door with you as easily? Theravada practice keeps a set for exactly that, called the four protections. Each one takes about a breath. The Buddha. Kindness. The body. Death. That last one sounds heavy for a Tuesday morning. Stay with it; it turns out to be the one that makes the other three matter.
screen: `PHONE, KEYS, WALLET.` → `FOUR THOUGHTS FOR THE DOOR.` → `THE BUDDHA. KINDNESS. THE BODY. DEATH.`

segments.voice: Each one is a short form of a longer subject from the forty. First, the Buddha. The old recollection begins, in Pali, Iti pi so Bhagava: such indeed is the Blessed One, worthy, fully awakened. It's a reminder that a person once did this, so it can be done. Second, kindness: may all beings be well, the heart of the metta practice. Third, the body, seen plainly through its parts: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin. Not to hate it; to loosen vanity and wanting. Fourth, death: certain to come, its time unknown. One way to see why they travel as a set: they cover the mind from four sides. Confidence, against losing heart. Warmth, against ill will. Plainness, against vanity. And urgency, against putting off what matters. The fourth is the one that gives the others weight. If the time is unknown, today's kindness can't wait for a better day.
screen: `THE BUDDHA: IT CAN BE DONE.` · `KINDNESS: MAY ALL BEINGS BE WELL.` · `THE BODY: HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.` · `DEATH: CERTAIN, TIME UNKNOWN.` · then, large: `FOUR PROTECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Touch your thumb to your first finger: the Buddha, awake, so it can be done. Middle finger: may all beings be well. Ring finger: hair, nails, teeth, skin. Little finger: death is certain, the time unknown. Then go round the hand again, slower, letting each touch carry its thought.
Four protective meditations: the Buddha, kindness, the body's nature, and death. Four short reflections that fit on one hand.
Keep close: four protections, one per finger, ready at any door. Day thirty-nine of the forty, done.

screen: `DAY 1544 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY SUBJECTS · DAY 39 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: FORTY WAYS TO MEDITATE. WHICH ONE IS YOURS?`

howItsDone: In Theravada practice the four protections (recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, the unattractive parts of the body and mindfulness of death) can be done briefly each day, sometimes before a longer sitting, as a short form of the fuller subjects.

notes: The name 'four protections' (caturarakkha) and its Devanagari spelling: confirm. The set is described as kept in Theravada practice without claiming how widely.

'One way to see why they travel as a set' (confidence, warmth, plainness, urgency against losing heart, ill will, vanity, delay) is an explanatory reading, not a quoted traditional list; confirm it is fair.
Iti pi so Bhagava is quoted in Pali (the original); the English that follows is a plain paraphrase of the opening words.
The myth item says the protections are not a lucky charm; Theravada also has protective chanting (paritta). A Keeper should confirm the reveal ('what they guard is the mind') doesn't dismiss paritta.
Senses shape: the practice is physical (thumb to each finger); the four taps are Ông Thanh's own habit in the storyline, not a claimed tradition.
